<margin># Solutions to the arguments.</margin>

The first point is clear. There is no doubt that, just as men can kill by divine permission, so too can they truly and really remove that member <note>referring to the phallus, a frequent subject in the *Malleus Maleficarum*</note> or others. But in such cases, demons do not operate through the witches of whom mention is now being made. Through this, the solution to the second point is also clear. But as for the argument that because God permits the generative power to be bewitched more [often] for the sake of something, therefore it is also permitted that such a member be truly and really removed, this does not hold because this does not happen by way of witchcraft, nor do witches even desire this when they perform such acts, since they do not have the power of restoring the member when they wish and know how. From which it is clear that it is removed not truly, but by the art of illusion. 

Regarding the third point, concerning the wife of Lot, we say: it was true and not by the art of illusion, but we are now speaking of the art of illusion. 

Regarding the fourth point, that demons can induce certain substantial forms and therefore can also remove them: it is said, concerning the magicians of Pharaoh, that they created true serpents. Demons can indeed produce certain effects around imperfect creatures with the aid of some other agent, which they cannot do around human beings, for whom God has greater care. According to that saying: "Is God concerned about oxen?" <note>1 Corinthians 9:9</note>. They can, however, always—as has been said—harm human beings truly and really by divine permission, or even by the art of illusion, and through this, the solution to the last argument is also clear.

<margin># Question 10: Whether witches operate upon humans by transforming them into bestial forms through the art of illusion.</margin>

Fourth, the truth itself is declared where people are also transformed into beasts. Regarding how this might happen, it is argued that it is not possible for this to occur. <term>XXVI. Q. V. Episcopi</term> <gloss>Decretum Gratiani, Part II, Causa 26, Question 5, Canon 12</gloss>, from the Council of Ancyra: Whoever believes that any creature can be changed for the better or the worse, or transformed into another species or into another appearance, except by the Creator himself, who made all things and through whom all things were made, is undoubtedly an infidel and worse than a pagan. And let us use the arguments of Saint Thomas in <term>II Sententiarum, Dist. VIII</term> <gloss>Commentary on the Second Book of the Sentences, Distinction 8</gloss>, as to whether demons can imprint things upon the bodily senses by deceiving them with illusions. Where he argues first that they cannot. For that form of a beast which is seen must exist somewhere, but it cannot exist only in the sense, because the sense does not have any species except that which is received from things, and a true beast does not exist there, according to the cited canonical authority. Nor again can it exist in the thing that is seen, such as a woman appearing as a beast, because two substantial forms cannot exist in the same subject at the same time and place. Therefore, since that form of a beast which is seen can exist nowhere, no illusory deception in the eye of the seer can occur, since vision must necessarily be terminated by some form. 

Furthermore, if it is said that this form exists in the surrounding air, this cannot be; firstly, because air is not receptive to any form or figure; and secondly, because it cannot remain the same air around that person due to its fluidity, especially as it moves; and also because such a transformation would thus be seen by everyone, which does not happen, since demons do not seem to be able to deceive the visions of holy men at least. Furthermore, the visual sense or visual power is a passive power. But every passive thing is moved by an active thing proportionate to it. Now, the active thing proportionate to the sense is twofold. One is as if originating the act, namely the object. The other is as if referring, such as the medium. But that form which is seen can be neither the object of the sense nor even the medium as if conveying it. Concerning the first, namely that it cannot be the object, because it cannot be taken from any thing, as was touched upon in the previous argument, since it does not occur in the sense from a thing received, nor in the thing itself, nor even in the air as in a referring medium, as was touched upon earlier in the third argument. <summary>This page concludes the responses to arguments concerning the physical manifestation of witchcraft and the "art of illusion," then introduces Question 10 regarding the transformation of humans into beasts, utilizing theological arguments from Saint Thomas Aquinas and canonical law.</summary>
